This card preserves only the documented October 15 health-policy answer. The available report gives no coverage mechanism, cost estimate, bill, or subsequent outcome. It also does not establish whether Trump had a separate proposal elsewhere; the description is limited to his answer at this event.

corrected_proposal.title: Trump and Hegseth Remove Senior Military Leaders in February 2025
corrected_proposal.description_short: Trump fired Joint Chiefs Chair C.Q. Brown; Hegseth also dismissed senior officers. The supplied impeachment-retaliation motive remains unsupported.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: On February 21, 2025, President Donald Trump fired Joint Chiefs Chairman Air Force Gen. C.Q. Brown Jr. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth then fired Navy Adm. Lisa Franchetti and Air Force Gen. James Slife, according to AP reporting. Reuters described Brown and five other admirals and generals as pushed out in the leadership shake-up. The supplied impeachment-testimony motive is not established by these sources and is omitted from this corrected account.
corrected_proposal.description_long: This corrected entry records a February 2025 change in senior U.S. military leadership. Reuters reported that President Donald Trump fired Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. C.Q. Brown on February 21 and described five other admirals and generals as pushed out in the same shake-up. The Associated Press reported that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth followed Brown’s dismissal by firing Navy Adm. Lisa Franchetti, then chief of naval operations, and Air Force Gen. James Slife, vice chief of the Air Force; AP also reported on changes to the services’ top military lawyers. The supplied record asserted that officers were removed because they testified against Trump in impeachment proceedings. The reporting reviewed for this corrected card documents who was dismissed, but does not establish that causal allegation or identify impeachment testimony as the reason. The account therefore names only the documented personnel actions and leaves motive unresolved. It does not characterize the changes as retaliation, a purge of witnesses, or proof of political loyalty. No conclusion about legality or resulting readiness effects is drawn. This correction preserves the dated leadership-change event while removing unsupported participants and motive.

corrected_proposal.title: Bondi Calls for DOJ Working Group to Review Trump and Jan. 6 Cases
corrected_proposal.description_short: AP reported that after her February 5 swearing-in, Bondi called for a DOJ group to review Trump and Jan. 6 prosecutions.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: The Associated Press reported that Pam Bondi was sworn in as attorney general on February 5, 2025, and hours later called for a Justice Department “weaponization working group.” AP said the group would scrutinize Jack Smith’s work and review prosecutions stemming from January 6. The report documents a review directive, not a January 20 order to dismiss cases against Trump allies.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On February 5, 2025, the Associated Press reported that Pam Bondi was sworn in as attorney general and, hours later, called for a Justice Department “weaponization working group.” AP said the group would scrutinize the work of special counsel Jack Smith, who had charged Donald Trump in two criminal cases, and review what Bondi described as “unethical prosecutions” stemming from the January 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol. The supplied original entry instead claimed that Bondi ordered DOJ to drop or suspend a broad set of cases against Trump allies on January 20, including fraud and campaign-finance matters. The date is incompatible with AP’s account of Bondi taking office on February 5, and the AP article describes reviews rather than case dismissals. This correction records the same-day directive AP documents and does not claim that cases were dismissed. It also does not treat the act of reviewing cases as proof of misconduct. The record does not establish which cases, if any, the working group later recommended for action or what outcomes followed.

corrected_proposal.title: Trump promoted a $59.99 branded Bible; $300 million in revenue is unsupported
corrected_proposal.description_short: Trump promoted the $59.99 God Bless the USA Bible; AP reporting does not substantiate the $300 million revenue claim.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: On March 26, 2024, Trump promoted the God Bless the USA Bible and urged supporters to buy it from a website listing the price at $59.99. AP later reported close to 120,000 copies shipped to the United States from China by late March and estimated about $7 million in potential retail sales at the minimum price. AP also cited a disclosure showing $300,000 in CIC Ventures Bible royalties, while noting the period and any additional payments were unclear. The $300 million revenue claim is unsupported by these reports.
corrected_proposal.description_long:
On March 26, 2024, Donald Trump promoted the “God Bless the USA Bible,” urging supporters to buy it from a website listing the price at $59.99. The website said Trump’s name and image were used under a paid license from CIC Ventures, a company he reported owning. The book combined a King James Version Bible with U.S. founding documents and the Pledge of Allegiance.

The original title’s $300 million revenue figure is not substantiated by the reporting reviewed here. In October 2024, the Associated Press reported that trade records showed close to 120,000 copies shipped from China to the United States between early February and late March. At the minimum retail price, AP estimated potential sales revenue for those shipments at about $7 million. AP also cited a financial disclosure showing $300,000 in Bible royalties earned by CIC Ventures, while stating that the disclosure period and any additional payments were unclear. Shipment estimates, potential retail sales, company royalties, and Trump’s total receipts are different measures; these reports do not establish total eventual sales or payments. The corrected entry records the promotion and licensing arrangement, removes the unsupported $300 million claim, and leaves final revenue and total royalties unknown.

corrected_proposal.title: Trump Pardoned Three Former Border Patrol Agents in December 2020
corrected_proposal.description_short: Trump pardoned former Border Patrol agents Ignacio Ramos, Jose Compean and Gary Brugman in December 2020.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: Trump pardoned Ignacio Ramos and Jose Compean on December 22, 2020, and Gary Brugman on December 23. The White House and Texas Tribune sources describe their separate convictions involving assault or deprivation of civil rights. The January 2025 clemency proclamation concerned January 6-related offenses, so the original date is corrected to the documented 2020 actions.
corrected_proposal.description_long: President Donald Trump granted full pardons to former Border Patrol agents Ignacio Ramos and Jose Compean on December 22, 2020, and former agent Gary Brugman on December 23. The archived White House statement about Ramos and Compean says they were convicted of assault, a firearm offense and deprivation of civil rights in connection with the 2005 shooting of a man near the U.S.-Mexico border. A Texas Tribune report describes Brugman’s 2002 conviction for deprivation of rights after he struck detained migrants; the report says he served more than two years in federal prison. These grants occurred in December 2020, not as part of Trump’s January 20, 2025 clemency proclamation. The Justice Department describes that later proclamation as covering offenses relating to the January 6, 2021 Capitol events. This correction preserves the earlier pardons and the documented conviction records while removing the unsupported claim that the agents were pardoned in January 2025 or that all cited cases were the same event. It does not infer why Trump granted clemency or state that the convictions were later vacated.

evidence_map.fact: The White House archive states Trump granted full pardons to Ignacio Ramos and Jose Compean in its December 22, 2020 statement.
evidence_map.quote: Today, President Trump granted full pardons to Ignacio Ramos and Jose Compean.
evidence_map.source_excerpt: Today, President Trump granted full pardons to Ignacio Ramos and Jose Compean. These former Border Patrol Agents have been supported by one hundred members of Congress, including Rep. Louie Gohmert, Rep. Steve King, Rep. Ted Poe, Rep. Paul Gosar, Rep. Brian Babin, as well as the U.S. Border Control Foundation and the Conservative Legal Defense and Education Fund. Both men served as Border Patrol Agents and put themselves in harm’s way to help secure our southern border with Mexico. On one such occasion in 2005, they stopped an illegal alien trafficking 700 pounds of marijuana. When the illegal alien—who was thought to be armed—resisted arrest, Mr. Ramos shot the suspect, who fled back across the border. For this, Mr. Ramos and Mr. Compean were charged and convicted of assault, using a firearm during a crime of violence, and deprivation of civil rights.

evidence_map.fact: The Texas Tribune reports Trump pardoned former Border Patrol agent Gary Brugman on December 23, 2020, and describes his civil-rights conviction.
evidence_map.quote: President Donald J. Trump announced 26 new pardons Wednesday, including one for Gary Brugman, a former U.S. Border Patrol agent who was sent to prison for nearly two years for violating the civil rights of a man attempting to cross the U.S. border into Texas.
evidence_map.source_excerpt: By Alex Samuels Dec. 23, 2020, 8:34 p.m. Central Updated Dec. 23, 2020, 8:34 p.m. Central. President Donald J. Trump announced 26 new pardons Wednesday, including one for Gary Brugman, a former U.S. Border Patrol agent who was sent to prison for nearly two years for violating the civil rights of a man attempting to cross the U.S. border into Texas. Brugman was convicted in 2002 and spent more than two years in a federal prison. On the campaign trail and in the White House, Trump has touted hard-line immigration policies that have drawn pushback from human rights groups. A day earlier, on Tuesday, Trump pardoned Ignacio Ramos and Jose Compean, two former Border Patrol agents who were convicted of assault. Ramos’ and Compean’s sentences had been commuted by then-President George W. Bush. Trump granted them a full pardon.

impact_proposal.confidence_reason: The pardon dates and convictions are supported by archived White House statements and reporting; the cited material does not establish harm caused by the pardons or damage to institutions.
impact_proposal.rationale: The three grants affected a small named group and created durable individual clemency effects, supporting reach 2 and persistence 3. The underlying convictions describe past offenses, not harm caused by the pardon itself; no post-pardon harm, institutional damage, procedural abuse, or private benefit is established here.
impact_proposal.basis: Full pardons for three former agents on December 22–23, 2020; the sources describe prior convictions but no resulting post-pardon outcome.
impact_proposal.notes: Editorial comparison only; ordinary clemency is not itself misconduct.
